name: background-sync
context: An application must keep working when it is not in the foreground — refreshing content, uploading telemetry, draining a write queue, reconciling local state with a server — under an operating system that will throttle, batch and defer all of it for battery and politeness. The pattern makes that work declarative: submit a request with explicit constraints, let the platform decide when it runs, and design the request to survive app exit, process death and device reboot without depending on exact timing.
benefits: Work survives app exit, process death and reboot, unlike coroutines, handlers and in-app timers
Constraints let the platform pick a good moment — unmetered network, charging, idle device — instead of the app guessing
Periodic and one-shot requests share one queue with one retry and backoff policy
Expedited work gives a latency-sensitive path with its own quota, so urgent sync does not starve behind routine sync
The web equivalents — Background Sync, Background Fetch and Periodic Background Sync — give the same behaviour with no install
tradeoffs: Execution time is not guaranteed and never exact — Doze, standby buckets and battery optimisers defer and batch freely
Standby buckets cap total runtime per window, so a rare bucket can allow roughly ten minutes of scheduled jobs per rolling day
Periodic work has a hard minimum interval (15 minutes on Android), which rules out fine-grained polling
Expedited work draws on a finite quota; running out degrades the request to ordinary or drops it entirely
Work that must finish within seconds is not a background-sync problem — it belongs in the foreground with a progress indicator
use_cases: Periodic content refresh for a news or feed app while it is closed
Queued uploads and telemetry flushing on unmetered networks only
Reconciling a local-first database with the server whenever connectivity allows
Cache warming and prefetch of content the user is likely to open next
Battery-gated maintenance such as compaction, cache eviction and index rebuilds
avoid_when: The work must complete within seconds — background execution cannot meet that latency
The result is needed to render the current screen, in which case it belongs on the foreground path
The platform offers no scheduling primitive for the target (a desktop app cannot rely on a service worker)
A continuous open connection is required — that is a different architectural choice, not background work
component_types: Work request: a declarative description of the work with its constraints, backoff and input data
Constraints: network type, battery-not-low, requires-charging, device-idle, storage-not-low — all must be satisfied
Scheduler: the OS service that persists and executes requests (JobScheduler on Android)
Worker: the unit that performs the work and reports result state
Expedited quota manager: the system-level budget that gates latency-sensitive work, with an out-of-quota policy
Backoff policy: retry schedule with criteria for system-initiated interruptions
anti_patterns: Using a Handler, Timer or coroutine for work that must survive the process
Starting a foreground service to run recurring sync, which the platform treats as user-visible and battery-hostile
Submitting requests with no constraints and wondering why battery drains and the scheduler batches everything
Enqueuing expedited work without an out-of-quota policy, so the request is silently dropped
Treating the periodic interval as a schedule rather than as the minimum gap between runs
best_practices: Treat every request as opportunistic and make the work idempotent, since it may run more often than expected
Express real requirements as constraints so the platform can batch intelligently
Choose the retry backoff criteria deliberately and handle system-initiated interruption separately
For web background sync, use waitUntil for anything that must finish and Background Fetch for anything long-running
Do not use background sync for durable work the user expects to happen — use explicit sync with a visible control
design_principles: Declare intent, let the platform schedule — never hand-roll timing
Express real requirements as constraints so batching is the platform's problem, not the app's
All background work is opportunistic and therefore idempotent, because it may run far more often than requested
Foreground latency belongs in the foreground; background execution has no latency guarantee to offer
Separate the durable queue from execution so a retry never duplicates a side effect
